ap_physics_1-f01.title: Block sliding down a rough incline

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=2\text{ kg}$ is released from rest on a rough incline that makes an angle $\theta=30^\circ$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $\mu=0.1$. The block slides a distance $d=5\text{ m}$ down the incline.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the block, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the block while it slides down the incline. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Three arrows from the dot: weight straight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline surface and pointing away from it, and kinetic friction pointing up the incline. The weight arrow is the longest and the friction arrow is shorter than the normal-force arrow.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the three forces: weight, normal force, and kinetic friction (no extra force such as a force down the incline)
common_errors: adds a force of motion down the incline

rubric_rows.criterion: Arrow directions are correct: weight straight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, friction up the incline
common_errors: draws the normal force vertical
draws friction down the incline

rubric_rows.criterion: Relative lengths are consistent: the weight arrow is the longest and the friction arrow is shorter than the normal-force arrow
common_errors: draws the normal force as long as the weight

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of the block down the incline in terms of $\theta$, $\mu$, and fundamental constants.
parts.model_answer: Perpendicular to the incline $N=mg\cos\theta$; along the incline $mg\sin\theta-\mu N=ma$, so $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law perpendicular to the incline: $N=mg\cos\theta$
common_errors: uses N = m g

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law along the incline: $mg\sin\theta-\mu N=ma$
required_elements: m g sin theta - mu N = m a
common_errors: uses the cosine for the component along the incline
adds the friction term

rubric_rows.criterion: Combines the equations to the correct expression $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)$
common_errors: leaves the mass in the final expression

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the block after it has slid the distance $d=5\text{ m}$ down the incline.
parts.model_answer: $a=4.05\text{ m/s}^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2ad}=\sqrt{2(4.05)(5)}\approx 6.36\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the acceleration (about 4.05) from the expression in part B
common_errors: uses the sine for both terms

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $v^2=2ad$ (or an energy equation) to find a speed of about 6.36 with units of meters per second
common_errors: forgets the square root

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The experiment is repeated on the same incline with a block of mass $4\text{ kg}$. Does the time for the block to slide the distance $d$ increase, decrease, or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The time stays the same. The mass cancels in $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)$, so the acceleration is unchanged and the time $t=\sqrt{2d/a}$ is the same.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the time stays the same
common_errors: states the heavier block takes less time

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the mass cancels, so the acceleration (and the time) does not depend on the mass
common_errors: argues only that heavier objects fall at the same rate without using the equation

ap_physics_1-f02.title: Block released from a height that stops on a rough section

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=0.5\text{ kg}$ is released from rest at a height $h=0.8\text{ m}$ above a horizontal floor on a smooth, frictionless curved track. At the bottom of the track the block slides onto a rough horizontal section whose coefficient of kinetic friction is $\mu=0.2$. The rough section is long enough that the block comes to rest on it. Blank energy bar chart templates (one per state, with a common scale) are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: In the energy bar charts below, for each of three states (the block at the release point, the block at the bottom of the track just before the rough section, and the block at rest on the rough section), draw bars for the kinetic energy $K$, the gravitational potential energy $U_g$ (zero at the floor), and the energy dissipated by friction as thermal energy $E_{th}$. Use the same scale in each chart.
parts.model_answer: At the release point: $U_g=mgh=3.92\text{ J}$, $K=0$, $E_{th}=0$. At the bottom: $K=3.92\text{ J}$, $U_g=0$. At rest on the rough section: $K=0$, $U_g=0$, and $E_{th}=3.92\text{ J}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Shows only $U_g$ (no $K$ and no $E_{th}$) at the release point
common_errors: shows kinetic energy at the release point

rubric_rows.criterion: Shows $K$ equal in height to the initial $U_g$ with $U_g=0$ and $E_{th}=0$ at the bottom of the track
common_errors: shows thermal energy on the frictionless track

rubric_rows.criterion: Shows $K=0$, $U_g=0$, and $E_{th}$ equal in height to the initial $U_g$ when the block is at rest
common_errors: shows the thermal energy smaller than the initial potential energy

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the distance $d$ the block slides on the rough section before it stops in terms of $h$, $\mu$, and fundamental constants.
parts.model_answer: Energy conservation on the track gives $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$; the work of friction on the rough section removes it all, $\mu mgd=\tfrac12mv^2$. Together $\mu mgd=mgh$ so $d=h/\mu$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses conservation of energy on the track: $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$ (or $v=\sqrt{2gh}$) at the bottom
common_errors: uses mgh = mv

rubric_rows.criterion: Equates the work done by friction to the kinetic energy lost on the rough section: $\mu mgd=\tfrac12mv^2$
required_elements: mu m g d = 1/2 m v^2
common_errors: omits the normal force in the friction work
uses a net force without the displacement

rubric_rows.criterion: Combines the equations to the correct expression $d=h/\mu$
common_errors: leaves the mass in the final expression

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the numerical value of $d$ for $h=0.8\text{ m}$ and $\mu=0.2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the distance (about 4.00)
common_errors: uses a wrong energy

rubric_rows.criterion: Reports the value with correct units of meters

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The block is released from twice the height $2h$ on the same track and the same rough section. By what factor does the distance the block slides on the rough section change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The distance doubles. From $d=h/\mu$ the distance is proportional to $h$ (the mass cancels), or equivalently the block starts with twice the energy and the same friction force removes it.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the distance increases by a factor of 2
common_errors: states the distance increases by a factor of 4 because the speed squared doubles

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $d\propto h$ from the derived expression, or with twice the initial energy removed by the same friction force
required_elements: twice the energy same friction force
common_errors: argues only that the block moves faster

ap_physics_1-f07.title: Claim about the friction force needed on a flat curve

stimulus.description: A car of mass $m=1000\text{ kg}$ drives at a constant speed around a flat, unbanked circular curve of radius $r=40\text{ m}$. The coefficient of static friction between the tires and the road is $\mu_s=0.5$. A student claims that if the car's speed is doubled, the friction force needed to keep the car on the curve is also doubled.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Do you agree or disagree with the student's claim? Justify your answer qualitatively without calculating numbers.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The friction force from the road is the net force toward the center of the circle and must equal $mv^2/r$, which depends on the square of the speed, so doubling the speed requires more than double the friction force.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim (the required friction force more than doubles)
common_errors: agrees because force is proportional to speed

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by identifying the friction force as the net force toward the center that provides the centripetal acceleration
common_errors: says an outward force balances friction

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by relating the required force to the square of the speed, $mv^2/r$, so the force changes faster than the speed
common_errors: says the force depends on speed to the first power

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the maximum speed $v_{max}$ at which the car can go around the curve without sliding in terms of $\mu_s$, $r$, and fundamental constants, and calculate its value for $\mu_s=0.5$ and $r=40\text{ m}$.
parts.model_answer: At the limit the maximum static friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu_smg=mv_{max}^2/r$, so $v_{max}=\sqrt{\mu_sgr}=\sqrt{(0.5)(9.8)(40)}\approx 14.0\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the centripetal requirement for the friction force: $f=mv^2/r$
common_errors: uses f = mv/r

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses the maximum static friction $\mu_sN$ with $N=mg$ on a flat road and sets $\mu_smg=mv_{max}^2/r$
required_elements: mu m g = m v^2 / r
common_errors: uses the weight with no friction coefficient

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v_{max}=\sqrt{\mu_sgr}$ and calculates about 14.0 with units of meters per second
common_errors: leaves the mass in the final expression

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The car is now loaded with cargo so that its mass doubles, and the road and the tires are unchanged. Predict whether the maximum speed at which the car can safely go around the curve increases, decreases, or stays the same, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: The maximum speed stays the same. The mass cancels in $\mu_smg=mv_{max}^2/r$, because the largest available friction force and the force required both increase in proportion to the mass.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the maximum speed stays the same
common_errors: states a heavier car needs a lower speed

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the mass cancels in the expression for the maximum speed (the friction capacity and the required force both scale with the mass)
common_errors: argues only that heavier cars are harder to stop

ap_physics_1-f08.title: Claim about a floating block in liquids of different density

stimulus.description: A uniform wooden block of density $\rho_b=600\text{ kg/m}^3$ floats at rest in fresh water of density $\rho_w=1000\text{ kg/m}^3$ with part of its volume under the surface. The block is then moved to a tank of salt solution of density $\rho_s=1200\text{ kg/m}^3$ and floats at rest there. A student claims that the block floats lower in the salt solution, with a larger fraction of its volume submerged, because the denser liquid is heavier.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Do you agree or disagree with the student's claim? Justify your answer qualitatively without calculating numbers.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. In both liquids the block floats at rest, so the buoyant force equals its weight, which does not change. The buoyant force is $\rho_{fluid}V_{sub}g$, so a denser liquid needs a smaller submerged volume to supply the same force.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim (less of the block is submerged in the denser liquid)
common_errors: agrees because the denser liquid pushes harder

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by stating that the block floats at rest in both liquids, so the buoyant force equals the block's weight in both (the same force)
required_elements: buoyant force equals the weight in both
common_errors: says the buoyant force is larger in the denser liquid

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by relating the buoyant force to the fluid density and the submerged volume, $\rho_{fluid}V_{sub}g$, so a larger density means a smaller submerged volume
common_errors: says the submerged volume does not depend on the liquid

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the fraction of the block's volume that is submerged in a liquid of density $\rho$ in terms of $\rho_b$ and $\rho$, and calculate the fraction submerged in the salt solution of density $\rho_s=1200\text{ kg/m}^3$.
parts.model_answer: At rest the weight equals the buoyant force, $\rho_bVg=\rho V_{sub}g$, so $V_{sub}/V=\rho_b/\rho$. In the salt solution this is $600/1200\approx 0.500$.
